poems.title: Epigram 184
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Palatine Anthology: Simonides; an hexameter followed by a nine-syllable:

This statue is the offering of Nicoladas of Corinth, who won the footrace at Delphi, who took sixty jars of oil in five prizes at the Panathenaea, whose rivals thrice upon end came not even before the oath-offerings at holy Isthmus; who won thrice at Nemea, four times at Pellene, twice at Lycaeus, and at Tegea, Aegina, and rocky Epidaurus, at Thebes and at Megara town; who at Phlius won the short course and the contest-of-five, and made great Corinth to rejoice.

poems.title: Epigram 185
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Planudean Anthology: The Same (Simonides):

This is the noble statue of the noble Milon, who kept his feet victoriously six times by the stream of Pisa.

poems.title: Epigram 186
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Diogenes Laertius Lives of the Philosophers: There have been three other men of the name of Arcesilaüs; . . . and another a statuary, to whom Simonides wrote the following inscription:

This is the statue of Artemis, the price of it two hundred Parian drachmas stamped with the goat, and the master that made it with aid of Athena was Arcesilaüs of Oaxus, son of Aristodicus.

poems.title: Epigram 187
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Palatine Anthology: Simonides:

From Alcon of Crete, the son of Didymus, this wreath to Phoebus for the victory in boxing at the Isthmus.

poems.title: Epigram 188
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos

poems.title: Epigram 190
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Pausanias Description of Greece [on a painting by Polygnotus at Delphi]: In this part of the painting there is a couplet of Simonides:

Polygnotus of Thasos, son of Aglaophon, painted the sack of the citadel of Troy.

poems.title: Epigram 191
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Palatine Anthology:

This was painted by Iphion of Corinth, and small blame to his hand; for work is far better than fame.

poems.title: Epigram 192
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
The Same: On the doors; by the same (Simonides):

The right hand of these doors did Micon paint, The right as you come out, Dionysius.

poems.title: Epigram 193
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Aristotle Rhetoric: For if an action exceeds what is expected of the actor's powers or years, or surpasses the common standard of those whom he resembles; or if it is performed in a certain way or at a certain time or at a certain place, it will acquire thereby a greatness, be it of beauty, of excellence, of justice, or of their opposites. Hence the inscription for the statue of the Olympian victor:

In the old days with a galling basket on my shoulders I used to carry fish from Argos to Tegea, [but now . . .]

poems.title: Epigram 194
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Palatine Anthology: Dedication by Simonides:

Pray that your gifts, O Cyton, may bring even as full joy to the holy Son of Leto who rules the marketplace of the fair dances, as the praise you have both of stranger and them of Corinth and the crown of thanks that has fallen to your lot.

poems.title: Epigram 195
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Herodian Words without Parallel [on 'I was']: Speakers of Attic say 'I was' and 'he was,' and Simonides uses the same form for the first person plural, as for instance in the Inscriptions:

We were once a hundred cups belonging to either city

poems.title: Epigram 197
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Athenaeus Doctors at Dinner: 'wreath': Apion in his book On the Latin Language declares that what is now called a wreath was anciently known by another name because it was used by the chorus-men in the theatres, who both wore a wreath themselves and competed for one; compare this passage in the Inscriptions of Simonides, where the word occurs:

Phoebus, who leads the singing of the children of Tyndareüs, is crowned with a wreath by these crickets of ours.

poems.title: Epigram 199
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Stobaeus Selections [on Time's nature and parts and of how many things he is the cause]: From the Inscriptions of Simonides:

The greatest touchstone of any work is Time, who showeth even the heart of a man beneath his breast.

poems.title: Epigram 200
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
Stobaeus Selections [on Time's nature and parts and of how many things he is the cause]: From the Inscriptions of Simonides:

. . . Sharp-toothéd Time grindeth all things up, aye, even the mightiest.
